structure.title: 1. Our Information-Extraction Method (1.1 segments, 1.2 extraction, 1.3 model performance)
1.4 Validating culture types; 1.5 Culture analyses and M&As
2. Comparing Different Stakeholder Groups' Perspectives (knowledge graph, frequency comparison)
3. Understanding Different Stakeholder Groups' Perspectives (sample overview, determinants, divergence)
4. Analysts' Perspectives on Culture and Stock Price Implications

observations.statement: The paper frames its core contribution as an information-extraction method: generative AI applied as a reasoning agent to extract cause-effect triples about culture from three corpora, organized into a knowledge graph. Regression analyses are presented as associations, not causal estimands.

Two generic threats of generative AI are named and addressed: look-ahead bias and hallucination. The authors argue the design mitigates look-ahead bias by construction because the task is extraction of contemporaneous perspectives, not out-of-sample prediction, and regressions use information available at report date.
observations.locator: Section 1.3, paragraphs on look-ahead bias and hallucination

observations.statement: Hallucination is addressed through prompt design: requiring explicit textual evidence and a stated reason for each relation, chain-of-thought steps constrained to the report content, and an explicit option to return N/A or empty arrays when no relation is supported.
observations.locator: Section 1.3; Table 1 panel A Q5 and Q7

observations.statement: Fixed-effects choices are motivated explicitly: firm by year fixed effects absorb time-varying unobservable firm characteristics affecting coverage decisions, and analyst fixed effects absorb innate skills or preferences about discussing culture.

Three text corpora are named with vendor and period: analyst reports from Thomson One Investext for S&P 1500 firms, earnings call transcripts from Capital IQ, and Glassdoor reviews via Revelio Labs. Sample formation steps and analyst-name matching to I/B/E/S are delegated to Internet Appendix sections.

Preprocessing steps are described in sequence: PDF to text conversion, C99 segmentation to restore paragraph structure, and a fine-tuned BERT boilerplate filter trained on most- and least-repeated segments from top brokers, with a median-probability retention cutoff reported in a footnote.

Culture-related segments are located by a three-stage funnel: keyword search, a BERT classifier trained on keyword-positive segments to find implicit discussion, and a generative-AI filter retaining only substantive culture discussion; the prompt for the filter is placed in the Internet Appendix.

A dedicated sample overview table reports counts of documents, firm-years and firms at each filtering stage (raw, with culture, with cause, with effect, with either, with both) for all three corpora, making the funnel transparent.

Table notes state the unit of observation, number of unique firms and analysts, and the sample period for each regression sample (firm-year, firm-analyst-year, analyst-executive and analyst-employee firm-year, report-level), and explain when fixed effects shrink the estimation sample.

The report-level event study sample excludes reports issued at the same time as earnings announcements, stated in the table note; the M&A sample is limited to deals with public acquirers and public targets.

The six culture types and standardized cause and effect entities are derived in two stages: manual review of frequent phrases guided by the literature, then BERT embeddings with hierarchical clustering to validate and refine categories; a second prompt maps free-text phrases to canonical entities using example phrases.

Tone is a three-valued GPT classification of each culture segment averaged to the report, firm-analyst-year or firm-year level; competing tone measures (FinBERT, Loughran-McDonald word list) are defined the same way for horse races. Nonculture tone for the rest of a report is FinBERT-based.

Divergence between stakeholder groups is measured as the Euclidean distance between share-of-mention vectors over a trailing three-year window, with the theoretical range stated; report-level versions concatenate type, cause, effect and tone components and are demeaned for interpretation.
All continuous variables are winsorized at the first and ninety-ninth percentiles and dollar values are expressed in 2020 dollars; count variables enter as log of one plus the count.

Abnormal returns are three-day cumulative abnormal returns from a market model with the CRSP value-weighted index; target price and revisions are scaled by the stock price fifty days before the report date, following a cited convention.
The local-analyst indicator is built by geocoding analyst office and firm headquarters addresses with a map API and computing Haversine distance against a mileage threshold.

Validation tables pair each culture type with two external markers and show a column without and with industry and year fixed effects; adjusted R2 and observations are reported per column; notes state clustering and control set.

Determinant regressions progress from industry plus year fixed effects to firm plus year fixed effects across columns, adding control blocks (strong culture, meetings, employee ratings) that shrink the sample; the text discusses which associations survive firm fixed effects.
Regression equations are displayed and numbered for the firm-year and firm-analyst-year specifications, with lagged regressors and the fixed-effects structure written explicitly.

For the report-level analyses, a panel A of the results table reports summary statistics (mean, quartiles, SD) of the key variables directly above the regression panel, which the text later uses for economic magnitude calculations.
observations.locator: Table 8 panel A; Table 9 panel A

observations.statement: The event-study table shows key report-level controls explicitly but collapses other analyst and firm controls into a single YES row.

Firm-level clustering is used for firm-year regressions and double clustering by firm and analyst for report-level regressions; the clustering level is stated in table notes but no reason for the choice is given in the text.
observations.quote: double-clustered at the firm and analyst levels

observations.statement: Extraction quality is benchmarked against human annotation of a random sample of segments, with accuracy, precision, recall and F1 defined in the table note and compared across three commercial LLMs of similar cost; the chosen model is justified on this comparison.
A footnote reports an ablation comparing chain-of-thought prompting with a single-pass prompt on the same annotated sample, used to justify the prompting strategy.

As a look-ahead check, firm, person and product names are masked with spaCy in a random subsample and tone agreement between masked and unmasked text is reported as evidence the model is not exploiting entity identities.

Each extracted culture type is validated by regressing an established external marker (ESG scores, Glassdoor ratings, patents, R&D, restatements, volatility, ROA, sales growth) on the type-specific tone, with the sign pattern read as construct validity.
Pearson correlation matrices for the regression samples are placed in the Internet Appendix and cited as a check that multicollinearity is unlikely.

Horse races between the GPT tone and FinBERT and dictionary tones are run for both research-output and market-reaction outcomes, placed in an Internet Appendix table and discussed in the main text in terms of incremental explanatory power and reported correlations among measures.
An untabulated alternative marker (Glassdoor culture and values rating) is mentioned in a footnote as a robustness check for one validation panel.

Additional analyses (horse race of stakeholder tones predicting performance, inter-analyst divergence determinants, consequences of divergence) are summarized in long footnotes with their tables in the Internet Appendix, each repeated with and without controlling for nonculture tone.

Heterogeneity in market reaction is examined through interactions of tone with an indicator for the deepest cause-effect analysis among peers and with divergence from management, employees or both; the standalone tone losing significance is interpreted as the reaction being conditional.

Determinant regressions are repeated separately for each culture type as dependent variable across columns, and divergence regressions separately for each stakeholder pair and each type, producing wide multi-panel tables.
observations.locator: Table 6 panel B; Table 7 panels B and C

observations.statement: Economic significance is stated as a one-unit tone change relative to the sample mean of the outcome, one SD changes in moderators, and basis points converted to dollar market value using average market capitalization; each arithmetic step is written out in a footnote.

The culture tone effect is benchmarked against the effect of nonculture tone in the same regression, with the authors arguing the culture effect is noteworthy given that nonculture text is more directly about financial performance.

Divergence patterns are interpreted through each stakeholder group's role and incentives; the governance-substitution interpretation is explicitly labelled suggestive and the section is called exploratory.

The link from culture analysis to prices is traced in two steps: first into analyst outputs (recommendations, target prices) and then into announcement returns, with the text distinguishing direct information effects from indirect effects via revisions.
Regression sections are framed as associations and exploratory analyses meant to generate future research, rather than causal claims.

Figures are a pipeline flowchart, a Sankey-style knowledge graph where node height and link width encode segment counts and effect nodes are shaded by tone, and a three-corpus frequency comparison with bars and colored markers; figure notes describe encodings and say Source: Authors' creation.

All regression tables use three-level stars, standard errors in parentheses, a YES/NO grid for fixed effects, adjusted R2 and observations, and a uniform note sentence on heteroskedasticity-consistent clustered standard errors and the Fama-French 12 industry definition.
The full LLM prompts (main chain-of-thought prompt and canonicalization prompt) are printed as a multi-page main-text table, with underlined sections indicating text omitted in the RAG second pass.

Full summary statistics are relegated to the Internet Appendix (numbered IA), while a variable-definition appendix (Table A1) in the paper lists each variable with data source, grouped by level of observation.
observations.locator: Section 3.1; Appendix Table A1; Table IA8

observations.statement: The introduction previews every result block in order, including some economic magnitudes, and then gives three numbered contribution paragraphs positioning the paper against culture, big data and analyst literatures; there is no roadmap paragraph.

The method section comes first and embeds validation and a first M&A application; descriptive comparison across stakeholders follows, then determinant regressions, then price-formation tests; each section ends with a summary paragraph and a bridging question to the next.

Robustness has no separate section; extra analyses live in Internet Appendix tables and are summarized in long footnotes, and implementation details for the extraction pipeline and sample formation are delegated to Internet Appendix sections A to C.

A Code Availability line after the conclusion gives a Harvard Dataverse DOI for replication code; earlier text says code is available upon request. Software named includes GPT-4o mini, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Gemini 1.5 Flash, BERT, FinBERT and spaCy.

All primary text data and most firm variables come from commercial vendors (Thomson One, Capital IQ, Revelio Labs, Refinitiv ESG, Audit Analytics, ExecuComp, I/B/E/S, CRSP, Compustat), with linkages to academic datasets (patents) and web APIs; no data-sharing statement is given beyond the code DOI.

The LLM pipeline is documented at the level of model choice, prompting strategy (chain-of-thought), retrieval-augmented context on demand with a relevance threshold from the BERT classifier, and output format (JSON triples with direction), with worked examples referred to the Internet Appendix.
Funding sources, editor, referees, discussants and seminar venues are listed on the title page, together with a pointer to supplementary material on the journal website.

gaps: No justification given for the clustering levels (firm; firm and analyst).
No discussion of LLM output stochasticity (temperature, repeated runs) or of prompt-version sensitivity beyond the chain-of-thought ablation.
No inter-annotator agreement reported for the human annotation benchmark.
No data availability statement beyond the code DOI; access procedures for commercial text corpora not described.
No preregistration, IRB or ethics statement.
No explicit external validity discussion (S&P 1500 firms, US sample).

reading.note: All 44 pages read, including the variable definition appendix (pages 39 to 41) and references (41 to 44). The Internet Appendix (Tables IA1 to IA12, Sections A to C) is a separate file and was not available; its contents are recorded only as cited in the main text.
